content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has highlighted the critical importance of self-care interventions, particularly in the context of cervical cancer screening and treatment. By 2030, there is an anticipated global shortage of 18 million healthcare workers, predominantly in lowand middle-income countries. Additionally, over 400 million people worldwide currently lack access to essential health services. During humanitarian crises, such as pandemics, routine health services are often disrupted, and existing health systems become overburdened. In such scenarios, self-care interventions can serve as an innovative strategy to strengthen primary healthcare, improve universal health coverage (UHC), and ensure continuity of health services that might otherwise be interrupted. In 2022, WHO updated its global normative guidance on self-care interventions for health and well-being. These recommendations are based on extensive consultations and a thorough review of existing evidence. Self-care interventions include evidence-based, high-quality medicines, devices, diagnostics, and digital products that can be used either fully or partially outside formal healthcare settings, with or without direct supervision by healthcare personnel. Cervical cancer remains a significant global health challenge, particularly in lowand middle-income countries, where socio-economic inequalities and health disparities limit access to screening and treatment services. This lack of access contributes to a high burden of cervical cancer in these regions. Most cervical cancer cases (99%) are linked to infection with high-risk types of human papillomavirus (HPV), which is sexually transmitted. Vaccination against specific high-risk HPV types is a key preventive measure, but many women in various countries are unable to access HPV vaccines. Cervical cancer is one of the most treatable forms of cancer when detected early and managed effectively. Regular screening and treatment of pre-cancerous lesions are essential to prevent the development of cervical cancer. WHO recommends using HPV DNA detection as the primary screening test, rather than visual inspection with acetic acid (VIA) or cytology, in screen-and-treat approaches for both the general population of women and women living with HIV. Self-sampling for HPV testing is an innovative approach that allows individuals to collect their own vaginal samples using a kit. This process can be done privately, either at home, in a healthcare facility, or another location. The collected sample is then sent to a laboratory for testing, and the results are returned to the individual. Self-sampling has been shown to significantly increase the uptake of cervical cancer screening services, nearly doubling participation rates. However, challenges remain in ensuring follow-up testing and treatment after self-sampling or regular screening. The self-sampling process typically involves using a single-use swab or cervical brush, which is inserted into the vagina and gently rotated for 10-30 seconds. The swab or brush is then placed into a provided collection tube containing a transport medium, sealed, labeled, and sent to a laboratory for analysis. WHO recommends making HPV self-sampling available as an additional option for women aged 30-60 years as part of cervical cancer screening services. Evidence suggests that self-sampling is both effective and acceptable to women. It can help achieve the global target of 70% screening coverage by 2030. Many women feel more comfortable collecting their own samples rather than undergoing screening by a healthcare provider. Where HPV tests are available as part of national programs, offering self-sampling as an option may encourage more women to access screening and treatment services, thereby improving overall coverage. To ensure the success of self-sampling initiatives, several factors must be addressed. Women must be provided with clear information about the benefits of cervical cancer screening and self-sampling, as well as detailed instructions on how to correctly collect a sample and what to do with it. Effective strategies must also be in place to facilitate follow-up testing and treatment after self-sampling or screening. Regulatory agencies should ensure the availability of high-quality self-sampling kits that are validated for use with HPV laboratory tests. National cervical cancer screening policies should be adapted to include HPV self-sampling as a complementary option, and appropriate laboratory infrastructure must be established to process the tests. Countries are encouraged to integrate HPV testing into their national guidelines for cervical cancer prevention and to consider including self-sampling as part of their existing screening and treatment strategies. Requests for HPV self-sampling kits can be made by healthcare workers or individuals themselves. By addressing these gaps and challenges, self-sampling has the potential to significantly improve access to cervical cancer screening and contribute to the global effort to reduce the burden of this preventable disease.
